item.title: Couple arrested with suspected drugs, housebreaking tools
item.description: A 41-year-old man and his 35-year-old wife are in Police custody after they were allegedly found in possession of white powder believed to be illicit drugs and housebreaking implements. The couple was arrested at around 1am yesterday after Police stopped and searched their vehicle at a checkpoint in Dokanaisuva.
item.content:encoded:
A 41-year-old man and his 35-year-old wife are in Police custody after they were allegedly found in possession of white powder believed to be illicit drugs and housebreaking implements.

The couple was arrested at around 1am yesterday after Police stopped and searched their vehicle at a checkpoint in Dokanaisuva.

Police say the vehicle was also found to have an expired wheel tax, while the man, who was driving, did not have a valid driving licence.

The couple remains in custody as Police investigations continue.

Police are expected to establish the nature of the suspected drugs and determine the circumstances surrounding the possession of the housebreaking implements.

item.title: Google project moves ahead, says Kamikamica
item.description: DEPUTY Prime Minister and Trade Minister Manoa Kamikamica says construction of Google’s data centre at Natadola is progressing well. Earlier landowners in Natadola raised concerns regarding transparency and the true scope of Google’s ICT and subsea cable landing facility.
item.content:encoded:
DEPUTY Prime Minister and Trade Minister Manoa Kamikamica says construction of Google’s data centre at Natadola is progressing well.

Earlier landowners in Natadola raised concerns regarding transparency and the true scope of Google’s ICT and subsea cable landing facility.

Government had since clarified and insists all legal and consultation steps were followed

“My advice is the landowners who own the land have sort of agreed to the investment,” Mr Kamikamica said.

“So I haven’t heard anything else since then.”

He said Google had ensured the project complied with Fiji’s laws, including requirements around engagement with landowners.

“Google’s a very responsible corporate player in the USA. And I know for a fact that they made sure they complied with all the laws of the country, including landowner engagement.”

He said Google was also working with communities around the data centre as part of its investment.

Mr Kamikamica said the facility would be powered by solar energy, creating an additional opportunity for landowners through the leasing of land for a solar farm.

He described the development as an exciting investment for Fiji and said Google’s presence would strengthen the country’s position in the telecommunications and information and communications technology (ICT) sectors.

“Those are the types of initiatives that this country is seeing. And I have to say with Google investing in Fiji, it’s really placed Fiji on the map when it comes to telecommunications and ICT.”

He expressed optimism about the future of Fiji’s ICT industry, saying the investment could lead to further opportunities in the sector.

item.title: PM Wale faces first no-confidence challenge
item.description: Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale’s three-month-old GREAT Coalition Government is facing its first major political test after a motion of no confidence was filed against him in Parliament. East Malaita MP and Minister of Home Affairs Manasseh Maelanga lodged the motion, with Parliament confirming receipt of the notice.
item.content:encoded:
Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale’s three-month-old GREAT Coalition Government is facing its first major political test after a motion of no confidence was filed against him in Parliament.

East Malaita MP and Minister of Home Affairs Manasseh Maelanga lodged the motion, with Parliament confirming receipt of the notice.

In the motion, Mr Maelanga accuses Mr Wale of making unilateral decisions without adequate consultation and of failing to take key matters through Cabinet.

The move has plunged the relatively new Government into political uncertainty, with parliamentary numbers expected to be crucial in determining whether Mr Wale can survive the challenge.

Mr Maelanga’s decision is particularly significant given his political relationship with the Prime Minister.

The two were part of the same political camp following the political standoff earlier this year and were initially rivals for the prime ministership.

Mr Maelanga eventually withdrew his candidacy on the morning of the parliamentary vote, paving the way for Mr Wale to secure the country’s top political office.

The latest challenge comes only months after Mr Wale led the opposition in successfully removing former Prime Minister Jeremiah Manele through a 26-22 vote in Parliament before forming the GREAT Coalition Government.

The motion was filed as Mr Wale was departing Solomon Islands for Palau to attend the Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting from August 30 to September 4.

Mr Wale is attending as outgoing Pacific Islands Forum chair and is expected to formally hand over the chairmanship to Palau President Surangel Whipps Jr.

The timing means Mr Wale faces a significant political challenge at home while representing Solomon Islands at the region’s premier leaders’ meeting.

Attention will now turn to the level of support Mr Maelanga can secure for the motion and whether the challenge exposes deeper divisions within the GREAT Coalition just three months after it took office

item.title: Seruiratu warns $10,000 kava fine could hurt ordinary families
item.description: Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu has called on the Government to reconsider proposed penalties under the Yaqona (Kava) Bill 2026, warning they could disproportionately affect farmers, villagers and small-scale sellers who depend on yaqona for additional income. Mr Seruiratu said he was concerned by reports that people selling yaqona without the required registration could face fines of up to $10,0
item.content:encoded:
Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu has called on the Government to reconsider proposed penalties under the Yaqona (Kava) Bill 2026, warning they could disproportionately affect farmers, villagers and small-scale sellers who depend on yaqona for additional income.

Mr Seruiratu said he was concerned by reports that people selling yaqona without the required registration could face fines of up to $10,000 or imprisonment for up to two years.

“A $10,000 fine and the prospect of two years in prison is an extraordinarily harsh penalty to hang over ordinary Fijians who may simply be selling a few bundles of yaqona to put food on the table,” he said.

Mr Seruiratu said yaqona provided an important source of supplementary income, particularly for families in rural and maritime communities.

“People sell yaqona to pay for groceries, school expenses, transportation, electricity, medical needs and other basic necessities,” he said.

He stressed that the Opposition was not against regulating the yaqona industry, saying there were legitimate reasons for protecting quality, improving traceability and preventing adulterated or falsely represented products from entering the market.

However, he said the law should distinguish between serious or repeated commercial breaches and small-scale selling by families.

“There is a significant difference between a deliberate commercial operator who repeatedly breaches the law and a rural family selling small quantities of yaqona to supplement household income.”

Mr Seruiratu said education, affordable registration and assistance with compliance should come before severe penalties.

He also raised concerns that the registration fee was yet to be determined and would instead be prescribed through regulations.

“The Government must guarantee that registration will be simple, affordable and accessible, particularly for people living in rural and maritime areas,” he said.

Mr Seruiratu also called for safeguards around enforcement powers, including entry into premises, inspection of records and collection of samples.

“There must be no room for intimidation, selective enforcement or unnecessary harassment of small operators,” he said.

He called on the Government to review the proposed penalties before the Bill becomes law.

“Government cannot continue talking about empowering SMEs and rural communities on one hand while creating laws on the other that could impose penalties worth many months, or even years, of income for some ordinary families.”

item.title: Constitution Review Commission to submit final report tomorrow
item.description: The Fiji Constitutional Review Commission will submit its final report on the review of the 2013 Constitution to President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu on Monday, August 31. In a statement released on its social media page, the Commission said the submission would mark the completion of its six-month mandate.
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Constitutional Review Commission will submit its final report on the review of the 2013 Constitution to President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu on Monday, August 31.

In a statement released on its social media page, the Commission said the submission would mark the completion of its six-month mandate.

“The report reflects the views, concerns and aspirations shared by Fijians throughout the consultation process,” the Commission said.

The seven-member Commission was formally commissioned by President Lalabalavu in March and was given until August 31 to complete its work and submit its final report. It is chaired by lawyer Sevuloni Valenitabua, with Ami Kohli, Dr Neelesh Gounder, Merewalesi Nailatikau, Dr John Fatiaki, Dr Salanieta Bakalevu and Conway Beg serving as members.

Under its terms of reference, the Commission was tasked with conducting meaningful consultations with Fijians and examining the effectiveness, relevance and implementation of provisions of the 2013 Constitution.

Its work included considering issues relating to governance, rights and accountability while ensuring the views of diverse and marginalised communities were taken into account.

The Commission conducted nationwide consultations, receiving oral and written submissions from individuals, communities, organisations and institutions.

By early July, consultation teams had visited more than 100 venues and received submissions involving more than 2,000 participants, before moving into the analysis and report-writing stage.

The review has also attracted debate over whether the six-month process provided sufficient time for public participation. The Commission rejected suggestions that the exercise was rushed, maintaining that extensive opportunities had been provided for Fijians to participate.

Monday’s presentation to the President will bring that process to its formal conclusion.

item.title: Cooperative diversifies operations
item.description: A farmers’ cooperative established more than seven decades ago is diversifying its operations with $14,000 in Government assistance to launch an equipment hire service in Votualevu, Nadi. Votualevu Credit Cooperative Ltd received the funding through the Cooperative Development Fund to purchase equipment that will be available for hire to members and residents for functions and community activities
item.content:encoded:
A farmers’ cooperative established more than seven decades ago is diversifying its operations with $14,000 in Government assistance to launch an equipment hire service in Votualevu, Nadi.

Votualevu Credit Cooperative Ltd received the funding through the Cooperative Development Fund to purchase equipment that will be available for hire to members and residents for functions and community activities.

Established in 1954 after local farmers pooled their resources to support one another, the cooperative has remained active across generations and now has 16 members. The new equipment hire service is expected to generate additional income for the cooperative while reducing the need for members and residents to travel to Nadi town to hire equipment.

Speaking at the event, Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica commended the cooperative for adapting its operations and identifying new opportunities for growth.

“I truly believe in the cooperative movement and small business movement and their ability to really transform lives in our country and help our people continue to live prosperous lives,” Mr Kamikamica said.

He said the Government support was aligned with the objectives of cooperative development by helping members create additional sources of income, strengthen their livelihoods and keep economic benefits within the cooperative. The initiative demonstrates how established cooperatives can diversify their income streams, strengthen their sustainability and provide services that meet the needs of their communities.

item.title: Legal Aid eligibility
item.description: THE Government is reviewing the $15,000 annual income threshold used to determine eligibility for Legal Aid, amid rising living costs. Acting Attorney-General and Justice Minister Siromi Turaga told Parliament this while responding to questions on the Legal Aid Commission’s means threshold. Currently, the $15,000 threshold is the maximum annual net disposable income generally used by Legal Aid to
item.content:encoded:
THE Government is reviewing the $15,000 annual income threshold used to determine eligibility for Legal Aid, amid rising living costs.

Acting Attorney-General and Justice Minister Siromi Turaga told Parliament this while responding to questions on the Legal Aid Commission’s means threshold. Currently, the $15,000 threshold is the maximum annual net disposable income generally used by Legal Aid to decide whether someone qualifies for legal assistance.

Mr Turaga said that threshold was used as part of the Commission’s eligibility means test and had been in place since the legal aid system commenced in 1998.

He said the $15,000 threshold had been in place for more than 25 years.

“During that period, Fiji has experienced significant changes in population, wages, household expenditure, and overall cost of living,” Mr Turaga said.

He said the economic circumstances faced by individuals and families today were different from those when the threshold was introduced.

Mr Turaga clarified that the assessment was based on net disposable income and not simply an applicant’s gross annual salary.

“The Director of Legal Aid has a discretion to consider providing assistance to an applicant whose disposable income exceeds $15,000, depending on the individual circumstances of the applicant.

“I support the review of the current means threshold.”

He said the objective of the review was to ensure the threshold remained appropriate in the current economic environment and that people who required legal assistance were not excluded because of outdated criteria.

item.title: Thousands to benefit from new mortuary
item.description: ABOUT 53,000 people in the Nadroga Navosa province are expected to benefit from the new Sigatoka Hospital mortuary built through funds raised by the region’s Australia-based diaspora. Nadroga Navosa Australian Community (NNAC) representative Tukini Tavui said the $130,000 project highlighted the significant difference the Fijian diaspora could make for their provinces.
item.content:encoded:
ABOUT 53,000 people in the Nadroga Navosa province are expected to benefit from the new Sigatoka Hospital mortuary built through funds raised by the region’s Australia-based diaspora.

Nadroga Navosa Australian Community (NNAC) representative Tukini Tavui said the $130,000 project highlighted the significant difference the Fijian diaspora could make for their provinces.

“The opening of the mortuary is a fitting demonstration of the spirit upon which the community was founded people living far from home remaining connected to their roots and working collectively to make a practical difference,” Mr Tavui said.

“The project demonstrates the important contribution that Fijians living abroad can make to development in their home provinces through organised community partnerships, fundraising and collaboration with institutions in Fiji.”

During the opening, Health and Medical Services Minister Dr Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu said for a long time Sigatoka residents had to travel to Suva or Lautoka to access the vital services.

“The old mortuary facility served us well with its nine berths, but as our community grew, we needed something better. This project was born to give our families the dignity, comfort, and peace they deserve, right here close to home.”

Dr Lalabalavu confirmed the ministry contributed $20,000 for electrical and engineering work.

The new facility features 18 berths, two fully equipped bathing bays, a dedicated viewing area and a chapel.
